standard.title: Turn-taking and active listening
standard.description: use interaction skills including turn-taking, speaking clearly, using active listening behaviours and responding to the contributions of others, and contributing ideas and questions
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can interact in informal and structured situations by listening while others speak and using some features of spoken language (AC9EFLY02). They have not yet applied the full set of interaction skills systematically — turn-taking, active listening, responding to others' contributions, and contributing ideas and questions as a coordinated set.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students use interaction skills including turn-taking, active listening, responding to others' contributions, and contributing ideas and questions in discussions.

nodes.label: Turn-taking and clear speaking
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can take turns to speak in structured discussions and speak clearly enough to be understood by the group.
nodes.minimum_width: Wait for their turn and contribute at least one idea, speaking at an audible volume and pace.
nodes.typical_width: Consistently take turns in group and class discussions, speak clearly with appropriate volume and pace, and wait without interrupting.
wider: Practise turn-taking in different group sizes — pairs, small groups, whole class — and discuss how expectations shift
Explore how turn-taking conventions differ across formal and informal discussion contexts

response_modes.reason: Turn-taking requires repeated practice in varied group configurations before it becomes habitual. Students need many opportunities to build the self-regulation needed for consistent, non-interruptive turn-taking.

success_criteria: Student waits for their turn before speaking in a discussion
Student's contribution is audible and clear to the group

nodes.label: Active listening behaviours
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can demonstrate active listening — attending to the speaker, making eye contact, showing they are following the contribution.
nodes.minimum_width: Demonstrate at least two active listening behaviours (e.g. eye contact, nodding, facing the speaker) during a discussion.
nodes.typical_width: Demonstrate a consistent set of active listening behaviours — eye contact, body orientation, nodding or other acknowledgement — across structured discussion activities.
wider: Discuss what it looks like from a speaker's perspective when the audience is and isn't actively listening
Explore how active listening behaviours may differ across cultural contexts
success_criteria: Student demonstrates at least two observable active listening behaviours
Student can name the behaviours and explain why they matter

nodes.label: Responding to and building on contributions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can respond to what others have said — acknowledging, agreeing, questioning or extending a previous contribution.
nodes.minimum_width: Respond to at least one contribution from another student, acknowledging what was said before adding their own idea.
nodes.typical_width: Respond to others' contributions in discussion, using language that acknowledges what was said (e.g. 'I agree with...', 'I also think...', 'But what about...') and adds a new idea or question.
wider: Practise restating another person's idea before responding — discuss how this changes the quality of the discussion
Explore how asking a question in response to a contribution extends the discussion in a different way than agreeing does

response_modes.reason: Responding to a contribution requires students to listen, hold what was said, and then connect their own response — a sequenced reasoning move. A simple scaffold ('I heard [name] say... and I think...') supports this coordination.

success_criteria: Student explicitly acknowledges a prior contribution before making their own
Student's response connects to what was previously said rather than introducing an unrelated idea
